amendments.rule: The definite direct-object marker `אֵת` (H853) has no English realization of its own and is normally its own `unrepresented` unit; that is the ruling on the large majority of its occurrences. It takes English only where the ASV spends a word on the object relation itself and no other morpheme licenses that word. Five families qualify. An English verb may reach its object through a preposition — *hearken unto*, *spake unto*, *inquire of*, *fight against*, *send for* — where that preposition exists only to attach the object to the verb; it is the marker's rendering, not the object noun's, and the marker heads on it. An appositional or resumptive marker may be rendered *even* or *to wit*. **But only a marker standing on the very phrase that English word introduces.** Where the ASV writes an appositional *even* or *to wit* before a phrase no marker marks, no morpheme licenses it and it is its own `added` unit under rule 30, whatever markers stand elsewhere in the clause: `וְחַקּוֹתָ עָלֶיהָ עִיר אֵת־יְרוּשָׁלִָם` → *portray upon it a city,* ***even*** *Jerusalem* gives *even* to the marker, which stands on the appositive itself, while `נָתַתִּי לְךָ אֵת־שְׁנֵי עֲוֺנָם לְמִסְפַר יָמִים שְׁלֹשׁ־מֵאוֹת וְתִשְׁעִים יוֹם` → *a number of days,* ***even*** *three hundred and ninety days* leaves the *even* `added`, because the clause's one marker stands on `שְׁנֵי עֲוֺנָם`, which the ASV renders bare. Do not reach across the clause for a marker to carry such a word, for the reason rule 42 gives about a surplus *and*: the word is written beside those renderings rather than inside one of them. **But an *even* the ASV writes inside another morpheme's own multi-word rendering is not an appositional *even* at all, and the preceding sentence does not reach it.** Where the ASV expands an extent or limit preposition as *even unto*, *even to*, *even till* or *even for*, the whole expression is that preposition's rendering and belongs to its unit, headed by rule 24 on the word carrying the relation — *unto*, *to*, *till*, *for* — and the *even* is neither `added` nor any marker's, whatever markers stand elsewhere in the clause: `וַיִּירַשׁ אֶת־אַרְצוֹ מֵאַרְנֹן עַד־יַבֹּק עַד־בְנֵי עַמּוֹן` → *from the Arnon unto the Jabbok* ***even unto*** *the children of Ammon* gives *even unto* to the second `עַד`, which is the morpheme the two words are written for. Read what the English word stands before, which is this rule's subtraction test again: an appositional *even* stands before a nominal that renames what precedes it, and this one stands before the object of the very preposition written beside it, so dropping it diminishes that preposition's rendering and nothing else. Two limits. Where a connective morpheme stands in the clause and the ASV writes a bare *even* for it, rule 14 governs and the word is the connective's; the corpus aligns a waw to *even* in 179 units and to *even unto* in none, so read which of the two the ASV has written. And where the ASV leaves the preposition's own relation unstated, rule 40 governs as before and there is no expression to place. The corpus aligns a preposition to *even unto* in 33 units and `עַד` to *even to* in 28 more, always headed on the second word. **Read that first limit as a count of the ASV's words against the morphemes standing in the phrase, and not as a test of whether the word *even* stands alone on the page.** Where a conjunction morpheme stands immediately before the limit preposition and the ASV writes *even unto*, *even to*, *even till* or *even for* at the head of that phrase, two English words answer to two morphemes and neither is a surplus: the waw takes the *even*, exactly as rule 14 gives the *even* of `וָיָמָּה` → *even unto the sea* to the waw written there, and the preposition takes the relational word alone, exactly as it does when the same phrase is written *and unto*. `וְעַד־בַּעַל גָּד` → ***even unto*** *Baal gad* divides that way, and it divides identically to the `וְעַד` of `וְעַד מִשְׂרְפוֹת מַיִם` → ***and unto*** *Misrephoth maim* standing in the same chapter, the waw taking whichever connective the ASV wrote for it and the `עַד` taking *unto* in either case. Count the phrase's connective morphemes against the ASV's connectives and read which pair of members each stands between, as rule 26 counts a `מִן … עַד` range's connectives and rule 42 counts waws against *and*s; a waw beside such an expansion takes the bare *even* and never the pair, which is what the corpus's count of no waw aligned to *even unto* records. The whole-expression reading of the preceding sentences governs where no connective morpheme stands beside the preposition, which is what `עַד־יַבֹּק עַד־בְנֵי עַמּוֹן` above is, and it governs a comparative or other preposition expanded the same way with no conjunction in the phrase: `כַּחוֹל` → ***even as*** *the sand* keeps both words with the `כְ`. So read whether a conjunction is present before placing the *even*, exactly as rule 14's own closing sentences direct for a coordinator and rule 51 for an *also*. And a marker on an object the ASV fronts before its clause and resumes inside it with a pronoun may be rendered *as for*: `וְאֶת־הַיְבוּסִי יוֹשְׁבֵי יְרוּשָׁלִַם לֹא־יָכְלוּ בְנֵי־יְהוּדָה לְהוֹרִישָׁם` → *And* ***as for*** *the Jebusites the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the children of Judah could not drive them out* gives *as for* to the marker, headed on *as* by rule 24, since the resuming *them* is the suffix's under rule 18 and nothing else answers to the two words. **The same limit governs that third family.** Where the ASV writes *as for* before a fronted phrase no marker stands on, no morpheme licenses the expression and it is its own `added` unit under rule 30, headed on *as*: `וּמַרְאֵיהֶם דְּמוּת אֶחָד לְאַרְבַּעְתָם` → *And* ***as for*** *their appearance, they four had one likeness* leaves the *as for* `added`, because `מַרְאֵיהֶם` is a bare noun and suffix with no marker and no preposition on it. Do not fold the expression into the fronted noun to avoid the `added`, for the reason just given about a surplus *even*, and do not reach for rule 33: that rule gives a supplied function word to a noun whose own case-function licenses it, and a topicalized nominal's fronting is not such a case-function. Where a morpheme does stand on the fronted phrase it takes the expression, whether that morpheme is a marker as above or a fronting `לְ` — `לָאוֹפַנִּים לָהֶם קוֹרָא` → ***As for*** *the wheels, they were called* gives *As for* to the `לְ` under rule 11. **And a marker on a direct object the ASV demotes to a role phrase takes the preposition written for it.** Where the ASV recasts the marked object as the role the thing serves and writes a supplied *for* or *as* before it, promoting the object's appositive to the English verb's object — `וְהֵבִיא אֵת־קָרְבָּנוֹ שְׂעִיר עִזִּים` → *he shall bring* ***for*** *his oblation a goat* — that word is the marker's and it heads on it, since the marked noun keeps its own English and nothing else in the clause answers for the preposition. Rule 33 is what governs the same clause written without a marker, and it says so in its own terms: a nominal with no preposition and no object marker on it takes the supplied word itself, as `וְהֵבִיא קָרְבָּנוֹ` → ***for*** *his oblation* and `יָבִיא קָרְבָּנוֹ` → ***as*** *his oblation* do. So read whether a marker stands on the noun before placing the word, and do not leave it `added`: one of the two morphemes always licenses it. **And a marker standing on a nominal the ASV construes as an adverbial adjunct takes the preposition written for that adjunct on those same terms.** Where the marked phrase is rendered not as the English verb's object but as an adjunct of place, time or manner, and the ASV writes a supplied preposition before it to state what the phrase contributes to its clause, that word answers to the marked phrase's relation and no other morpheme in the phrase carries it: the marker takes it and heads on it, while the noun keeps its own English. `וְשָׁפַט אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵל אֵת כָּל־הַמְּקוֹמוֹת הָאֵלֶּה` → *and he judged Israel* ***in*** *all those places* gives *in* to the second marker, the first marker standing on the verb's own object and going `unrepresented` as usual. Read the condition and not the lemma of the preposition, exactly as rule 40 directs: *in*, *on*, *at*, *after* and *according to* are read alike, and the corpus aligns an object marker to *according to* at HAG.2.5 and JDG.11.39 and to *at*, *about*, *after*, *on* and *upon* elsewhere. Two limits. A preposition the English verb's valency needs to reach its own object is the first family's and not this one, so ask whether the marked phrase is what the English verb reaches before placing the word. And where the ASV renders the marked adjunct bare, nothing is spent on the relation and the marker is `unrepresented` as usual. Test by subtraction: drop the English word and ask which morpheme has lost its rendering. If nothing but the object relation is diminished, the marker takes the word; if the ASV writes the object bare — *he built the house* — the marker is `unrepresented`. Do not confuse H853 with its homograph the preposition `אֵת` *with* (H854), which is an ordinary preposition aligning by rule 11.
amendments.why: 1SA.7.16 renders `אֵת כָּל־הַמְּקוֹמוֹת הָאֵלֶּה` as *in all those places*, a marked nominal the ASV demotes to a locative adjunct. None of rule 16's four families reaches it: the phrase is not what the English verb *judged* reaches, it renames nothing, it is not fronted and resumed, and it is not a role phrase. Rule 33 cannot take the word either, since its own third limit hands a word an object marker stands to take back to rule 16, so the contract as written left the *in* unplaceable and mildly self-contradictory. The corpus already carries the widening: object markers are aligned to *according to* at HAG.2.5 and JDG.11.39, and to *at* (GEN.24.57, JOS.9.14), *about* (EXO.19.23, JOS.19.14), *after* (DEU.22.2, HOS.2.7), *on* and *upon* — renderings the four families do not account for. The amendment names the fifth family, keeps the rule's own governing test (a word spent on the relation that no other morpheme licenses), and adds the two limits that stop it swallowing family one or a marker whose adjunct the ASV renders bare. Everything else in rule 16 is reproduced unchanged, including the *even unto* count and the rule 33 boundary.

conventions: levaddo -> *only* (1SA.7.3, 1SA.7.4): the preposition and baddo fuse under rule 30, since one English word carries the pair, and the unit heads on the construct noun bad. The pronominal suffix is no part of that fusion and is its own `unrepresented` unit, the ASV writing no pronoun for it — the *him* of *serve him* in 7.3 is the verbal object suffix, and the object in 7.4 is the written divine name.

A compound proper name that MACULA segments into two source tokens (Kiriath-jearim in 7.1 and 7.2, Beth-car in 7.11, Eben-ezer in 7.12, Beth-el in 7.16) takes one English word of the name per token, and whatever relational or determining English the phrase carries joins the first token's unit: the chain's *of* in 7.1 goes with *Kiriath*, and the second token takes only its own word.

A cardinal echad or achat standing on a written noun where the ASV writes only an indefinite article (7.9 tleh chalav echad -> *a sucking lamb*, 7.12 even achat -> *a stone*): the *a* belongs to the noun under rule 15 and the numeral is its own `unrepresented` unit. Rule 15's carve-outs give a numeral standing in the phrase a distributive *each* or *every*, and rule 31 gives a substantival numeral its *one*, but neither reaches an indefinite article written before a noun the Hebrew writes. BSB represents the numeral in both places; that is the convention difference and not an error.

And a marker on an object the ASV fronts before its clause and resumes inside it with a pronoun may be rendered *as for*: `וְאֶת־הַיְבוּסִי יוֹשְׁבֵי יְרוּשָׁלִַם לֹא־יָכְלוּ בְנֵי־יְהוּדָה לְהוֹרִישָׁם` → *And* ***as for*** *the Jebusites the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the children of Judah could not drive them out* gives *as for* to the marker, headed on *as* by rule 24, since the resuming *them* is the suffix's under rule 18 and nothing else answers to the two words. **The same limit governs that third family.** Where the ASV writes *as for* before a fronted phrase no marker stands on, no morpheme licenses the expression and it is its own `added` unit under rule 30, headed on *as*: `וּמַרְאֵיהֶם דְּמוּת אֶחָד לְאַרְבַּעְתָם` → *And* ***as for*** *their appearance, they four had one likeness* leaves the *as for* `added`, because `מַרְאֵיהֶם` is a bare noun and suffix with no marker and no preposition on it. Do not fold the expression into the fronted noun to avoid the `added`, for the reason just given about a surplus *even*, and do not reach for rule 33: that rule gives a supplied function word to a noun whose own case-function licenses it, and a topicalized nominal's fronting is not such a case-function. Where a morpheme does stand on the fronted phrase it takes the expression, whether that morpheme is a marker as above or a fronting `לְ` — `לָאוֹפַנִּים לָהֶם קוֹרָא` → ***As for*** *the wheels, they were called* gives *As for* to the `לְ` under rule 11. **And a marker on a direct object the ASV demotes to a role phrase takes the preposition written for it.** Where the ASV recasts the marked object as the role the thing serves and writes a supplied *for* or *as* before it, promoting the object's appositive to the English verb's object — `וְהֵבִיא אֵת־קָרְבָּנוֹ שְׂעִיר עִזִּים` → *he shall bring* ***for*** *his oblation a goat* — that word is the marker's and it heads on it, since the marked noun keeps its own English and nothing else in the clause answers for the preposition. Rule 33 is what governs the same clause written without a marker, and it says so in its own terms: a nominal with no preposition and no object marker on it takes the supplied word itself, as `וְהֵבִיא קָרְבָּנוֹ` → ***for*** *his oblation* and `יָבִיא קָרְבָּנוֹ` → ***as*** *his oblation* do. So read whether a marker stands on the noun before placing the word, and do not leave it `added`: one of the two morphemes always licenses it. **And a marker standing on a nominal the ASV construes as an adverbial adjunct takes the preposition written for that adjunct on those same terms.** Where the marked phrase is rendered not as the English verb's object but as an adjunct of place, time or manner, and the ASV writes a supplied preposition before it to state what the phrase contributes to its clause, that word answers to the marked phrase's relation and no other morpheme in the phrase carries it: the marker takes it and heads on it, while the noun keeps its own English. `וְשָׁפַט אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵל אֵת כָּל־הַמְּקוֹמוֹת הָאֵלֶּה` → *and he judged Israel* ***in*** *all those places* gives *in* to the second marker, the first marker standing on the verb's own object and going `unrepresented` as usual. Read the condition and not the lemma of the preposition, exactly as rule 40 directs: *in*, *on*, *at*, *after* and *according to* are read alike, and the corpus aligns an object marker to *according to* at HAG.2.5 and JDG.11.39 and to *at*, *about*, *after*, *on* and *upon* elsewhere. Two limits. A preposition the English verb's valency needs to reach its own object is the first family's and not this one, so ask whether the marked phrase is what the English verb reaches before placing the word. And where the ASV renders the marked adjunct bare, nothing is spent on the relation and the marker is `unrepresented` as usual. Test by subtraction: drop the English word and ask which morpheme has lost its rendering. If nothing but the object relation is diminished, the marker takes the word; if the ASV writes the object bare — *he built the house* — the marker is `unrepresented`. Do not confuse H853 with its homograph the preposition `אֵת` *with* (H854), which is an ordinary preposition aligning by rule 11.
amended.why: 1SA.7.16 renders `אֵת כָּל־הַמְּקוֹמוֹת הָאֵלֶּה` as *in all those places*, a marked nominal the ASV demotes to a locative adjunct. None of rule 16's four families reaches it: the phrase is not what the English verb *judged* reaches, it renames nothing, it is not fronted and resumed, and it is not a role phrase. Rule 33 cannot take the word either, since its own third limit hands a word an object marker stands to take back to rule 16, so the contract as written left the *in* unplaceable and mildly self-contradictory. The corpus already carries the widening: object markers are aligned to *according to* at HAG.2.5 and JDG.11.39, and to *at* (GEN.24.57, JOS.9.14), *about* (EXO.19.23, JOS.19.14), *after* (DEU.22.2, HOS.2.7), *on* and *upon* — renderings the four families do not account for. The amendment names the fifth family, keeps the rule's own governing test (a word spent on the relation that no other morpheme licenses), and adds the two limits that stop it swallowing family one or a marker whose adjunct the ASV renders bare. Everything else in rule 16 is reproduced unchanged, including the *even unto* count and the rule 33 boundary.

report: Checked all 40 candidate lemma groups and read the dump end to end for `added` units, which the table cannot see. No cross-verse split: every multi-treatment bucket is licensed by what the ASV wrote.

Waw buckets differ only by which connective was written, by none being written (apodosis waws at 7.7 twice, 7.10, 7.12, 7.16), or by the rule 55 coordinator-plus-subordinator pair (7.7 twice, 7.10), all headed on the coordinator. 7.2's two that-words are divided correctly — the temporal one to the infinitive as rectum of mi-yom under rule 52, the apodosis one to its own waw under rule 45 — and 7.3's `then` is added because that apodosis writes no conjunction at all.

Preposition-plus-construct fusions are uniform: li-fney (7.6, 7.10), mi-pney (7.7) and mi-dey (7.16) head on the construct noun; me-et (7.14) and mi-tachat (7.11) head on the governing preposition under rule 23's second sentence; mi-tochchem (7.3) is split because the ASV spent a word on each morpheme.

The five added units are one consistent judgment: supplied object *it* at 7.6, 7.7 and 7.12 (no object morpheme in those clauses, unlike 7.1 where the suffix takes it), the supplied apodosis *then* at 7.3, and the supplied subject-plus-verb *they came* at 7.11, correctly one unit under rule 2. Nothing comparable was folded into a licensing morpheme elsewhere.

Reviewed and accepted, but recorded here because the unit carries no rule 8 note: 7.11 gives *out* to yatsa as a phrasal particle and a bare *of* to min, where 7.3, 7.8 and 7.14 give *out of* whole to min. The difference is licensed — *went* alone does not write the going-out, while *deliver out* is not an English verb — but the competing reading is materially available and should be named if that verse is ever revised.

7.13's lo yasfu od writes two morphemes of repetition against one English *more*. The word went to od, whose lexeme it writes, leaving yasaf unrepresented; that is rule 56's own count (source verbs against English words) resolved by rule 24, and the unit names the competing reading, so no rule text was added for it.

BSB: no genuine error. The recurring classes (object markers, articles, unrendered waws and prepositions) are the documented convention differences. The three singletons are decided against BSB by the contract itself — the levaddo suffix by rule 30's own exclusion of a suffix from the fusion, and the two cardinals by rule 15, whose carve-outs give a numeral *one*, *each* or *every* but never the indefinite article.

One amendment returned: 7.16 gives *in* to the marker standing on et kol ha-meqomot ha-elleh, which none of rule 16's four families reaches while rule 33 defers back to rule 16 wherever a marker stands. Rule 16 is widened to a fifth family rather than left with a word no rule can place.
